A prominent American authority says :
Canada has resources equalling, if not exceeding, those of the United States, in agricultural and mineral wealth and in industrial possibilities. It has millions of acres of fertile farming land, rich mineral deposits, and transportation possibilities far ahead of ours. . . It does one good to see the crops they are raising up there. Wheat, barley, and oats are raised in immense quantities, and occasional patches of good corn. . . . Canada will develop pro rata the same way as the United States has grown.

Then we have the authority of the Department of the Interior for the following : Wheat has been successfully raised at Fort Simpson in latitude 62 degrees north, which is as far north-west of Winnipeg as Winnipeg is north-west of New York. Rye and oats are grown 200 miles farther north, and 200 miles still farther north barley and potatoes are successfully produced.
I stated that one of the conditions for the welfare of the inhabitants of the country is the producing capacity of the country. Another is its exporting capacity. The province of British Columbia has that capacity to a very large extent. Not only has it large exporting capacity, but it has great facilities as regards foreign commerce. The ports of Vancouver, Victoria, New Westminster, Port Simpson, and whatever other ports may be opened by the extension of this road have advantages far in excess of those of Puget Sound ports, Oregon and San Francisco. When I show you the extent of the exports from Puget Sound and the Oregon and the California ports, which are not so favourably situated so far as the wheat belts are concerned as are our Pacific coast ports, you will readily see the tremendous advantage to the western ports of Manitoba and the North-west Territories which will be conferred by the Grand Trunk Pacific road. The wheat exports from the Pacific coast ports in 1901 amounted to some 36,000,000 bushels; the flour exports from Puget Sound and from Seattle and Tacoma amounted to some 2,000,000 ban-els. Full particulars of these exports can be found in the American Trade and Navigation Returns of this year. From Montreal, Portland and St. John during tlie same period, 30,941,000 bushels of wheat were exported. From San Francisco alone there were 14,000,000 bushels exported. Those of you who are familiar with the geography of the western part of the continent will recollect that the Coast and the Cascade ranges of the Rocky mountains are further removed from the American coast than they are from the Canadian Pacific coast. As you go north the range converges to the Pacific coast, not only converges to the Pacific coast when it gets into the province of British Columbia, but it gets lower in altitude, affording an easy access across and low grades, and it comes within a few hundred miles of Port Simpson. So that the great wheat belt of the North-west Territories extends to within a few hundred miles of Port Simpson as against a distance of some thousands of miles from the western wheat belts which are tributary to the ports of San Francisco and Puget Sound and Oregon. It is therefore obvious that the great cost of the exports of western wheat of the United States to the Pacific coast ports is far in excess of the cost of the export of wheat of the Canadian belt to the Pacific coast and from there to the foreign ports. The competition that will be afforded by the Grand Trunk Pacific in rates will enable
the great wheat belt of the North-west Territories to be tapped. The wheat and grain belt of Canada will be within easy and cheap distance of the markets of the world. The Asiatic market we all know is growing in importance. The Puget Sound ports export large quantities of produce raised in territory similar to that of British Columbia and along which this road will traverse. They are exporting large quantities of their products to China, Japan and other ports of Asia. The port of San Francisco last year sent to China products of the value of $16,703,000, and to Japan, valued at $4,000,000. China, Japan and the Asiatic ports are .five or six hundred miles perhaps a thousand miles nearer us than they are to the American ports which have this splendid export trade already. All we want is some cheaper means of getting our wheat to the Pacific coast. It is absurd to say that by the Canadian Pacific Railway, great as are the advantages which it affords to the coast, you can haul wheat across the Rocky mountains and over the grades which characterize this road in competition with the Great Northern and the Northern Pacific roads. There is no question that an impetus will be given to the exports of wheat by way of the Pacific ocean that is almost inconceivable at the present time. In addition to all the other advantages to which I have referred, we have open ports the year round; so that I am not over sanguine in expecting that within ten years the bulk of the export of grain from the Dominion of Canada, and perhaps from the American continent, will be by way of the Pacific coast and by our own Pacific ports.
In what way will the building of a road from Winnipeg to Moncton decrease the expense of sending wheat from the wheat belt to the Pacific ocean?

As I stated in my opening remarks, I am quite satisfied to leave the justification of the action of the government respecting the Moncton and Winnipeg branch to the gentlemen who have preceded me. It would be a work of supererogation on my part to add one word to what has been "so ably said by the gentlemen who have treated that point. There is still another justification for the extension of the road to the Pacific coast and that is the matter of freight rates. The province of British Columbia is suffering at the present time, and unless this Grand Trunk Pacific road is extended or we have some other line to the coast, we will continue to suffer from excessive freight rates. To-day you can send farm implements or any other products to the Antipodes cheaper than you can send them to Vancouver or to Edmonton. That is a condition of affairs that ought not to exist, and the present administration are proceeding to remedy that grievance. The passenger rate in British Columbia from station to station is five cents, while east of
Manitoba and. as far as Nova Scotia, pass' eager rates are only three and two -cents.
Did the hon. gentleman vote for a two cent passenger rate to the Pacific coast that was moved here the other night 7

I have always had regard, in a matter of that kind, to the methods by which a thing is introduced into the House, and particularly to the individual who introduced it. So, having regard to both those circumstances, I thought it was not incumbent upon me seriously to consider the pro-position made by the hon. gentleman at that time. Now, in addition to these considerations to which I have referred, there is another very important element in our favour, aud that is the climate. Between latitude 49 and 59, which embraces pretty nearly the whole province of British Columbia, we find Great Britain, the Northwest of France, Belgium, Holland, North Germany, Prussia, Denmark, South Sweden, the Baltic provinces, the coast of Russia and the Gulf of Finland. I suppose there is no man in this House but knows what that means, that within these latitudes on the continent of Europe, is contained what is said to be the cradle of civilization, producing the sturdiest types of humanity. There is no reason in the world why, with the influx of people which the Minister of the Interior is assuring us in that province, and the facilities afforded by the government of which this project is merely an earnest, we will have in that province the most populous and most prosperous part of the Dominion of Canada within a very short period.
Generally speaking, we will not only render assistance by the construction of this line in the development of that important part of Canada, but by the development throughout the whole of Canada which will result from the adoption of this proposition we will bring back some if not all of the 1,183,225 Canadians who are in the United States to-day, according to the census returns of the United States of last year. There are 1,183,225 Canadians in the United States, 787,798 of whom come from provinces outside of the province of Quebec, while 395,427 are from the province of Quebec. There are 1,183,225 stalwart, worthy Canadians who want to return to Canada and who will return if the resources of this country are made known and facilities are provided for their development. I shall not take up the time of the House any farther. I should like extremely to dilate upon the very alluring topic of the position of the province of British Columbia in relation to the other' provinces in the Dominion of Canada, but in view of the long speeches that we have already heard and in view of the fact that there are a number of hon. gentlemen who wish to speak, I will conclude by reciting a piece of advice that was given
many years ago by that eminent philosopher Bacon. He said :
That which is past is gone and irrevocable and wise men have enough to do with things present and to come ; therefore they do but trifle with themselves that labour in past matters.
I, therefore, trust that hon. gentlemen on tile other side who may see fit to address the House will let bygones be bygones, and devote a little more time to present conditions, and to the future.

Mr. Speaker. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Morrison) who has just addressed the House, like a number of his predecessors, seems to make a point of discussing everything except the resolution before the House. He has given us a very beautiful description, in part, of British Columbia. Other hon. gentlemen have portrayed in choice language the beauties of parts of the provinces of New Brunswick and Quebec. Extracts have been read from clergymen's essays and reports have been presented covering the ground all the way from Labrador coast to James bay, and hon. gentlemen have discussed everything but the merits of their measure. These hon. gentlemen seem to take it for granted that they have discovered there is a climate in Canada, that there is soil, and that there is an opportunity of building another transcontinental road. I am not surprised at the language we now find them indulging in. These hon. gentlemen have for many a long year been engaged in belittling this country, and in providing speeches to be used by our friends in Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas and other southwestern states to deter emigrants from going to Canada, and It is, therefore, difficult even yet for some of their own friends to have faith in Canada. I want to point out to these hon. gentlemen, however, that it is quite unnecessary for them to speak to the country upon this topic as far as the Liberal-Conservative party is concerned. I am merely one member of the Liberal-Conservative party, but I want our hon. friends to recall to mind what they must well know, that the Conservative party have always pointed out the advantages of Canada, that they have always had faith in our great North-west, that they have always recognized that there is a large tract of fairly settleable country in the northern parts of Ontario and Quebec, and that it is possible to get a line-I will not say a short line-of railway from Levis south-westerly or easterly down through the province of New Brunswick. These hon. gentlemen are very far behind the times. If they go up to the Railway Committee room and look at the map they will see that there are at least a dozen charters authorizing the construction of railways by routes which are marked across the continent of North America, showing that for many a long year there are men in Canada who

have had faith in the country, and who recognized the fact that at some future date there will be another transcontinental line running across the Dominion. My hon. friend from British Columbia, as I said, has devoted himself chiefly to a description of his adopted province, and I must congratulate him upon his effort. But, how. the southern part of British Columbia wilt' be benefited by the construction of a railway three or four hundred miles north is something that I fail to see. I also fail to see what his quotation from the Vancouver newspaper edited by Mr. Cotton has to do with this matter. Mr. Cotton, as he himself says, had not read the contract and practically knew nothing about it. What Mr. Cotton speaks of is what every man in Canada who is cognizant of the advantages of this country should welcome and that is a proper scheme of opening up our own country. But, Sir, in discussing the development of the country we are not at all endorsing the iniquitous contract which is now before the House. The last speaker remarked that this contract was drawn with an eye single to promote the interests of British Columbia. I regret that he did not show where the single eye was, but I am glad that there is one part of the Dominion of Canada that the contract is drawn with the object of benefiting. It certainly is not the province of Nova Scotia, it is not the province of New Brunswick, it undoubtedly is not Quebec nor Ontario, it cannot be the North-west Territories ; therefore, as our hon. friend says, it is singly drawn for the benefit of British Columbia, and he regrets the delay in the execution of the terms of the contract by speeches such as that which has been delivered by my hon. friend for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox). I do not think that my hon. friend from South Simcoe has occupied any more of the time of this House than the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) or the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) on the other side of the House. One of these hon. gentlemen took about two days of the time of the House, and the other a day and a half, and I am satisfied to leave the country to judge between the speeches of these three hon. gentlemen. If there is not more solid, logic, more fact and more criticism in the speech of my hon. friend from South Simcoe than in the de-. fence of the measure contained in the two speeches of these hon. gentlemen, I will let the hon. gentleman's remarks pass unchallenged. My hon. friend from British Columbia took up the contract and he read a few paragraphs from it. One section of which he spoke particularly was section 10, and he also referred to the deposit of $5,000.000. However, as I propose to take this matter up as I proceed. I will not now refer to his remarks upon that point at any further length. I want to point out to our hon. friends opposite that the Liberal-Conserv-

ative party is not criticising the route of this railway. The Liberal-Conservative party has long been upholding the advantages of the Dominion of Canada and the various advantages both of the east and the west. It is not the question of route, but it is the question of the terms of the contract and the effect this contract will have upon the finances and the development of the country that we are basing our criticism upon, or at least I am criticising that feature of the proposition, and I think in that I voice the general sentiment of the friends of the Liberal-Conservative party, both in the House and out of it. We are not belittling the soil of the province of New Brunswick, of Quebec, or of Ontario-very far from it. On the contrary, the Liberal-Conservative party has been the leader in this House in drawing attention to the advantages of this country. For many long years our hon. friends opposite were unfortunately engaged in belittling Canada. We are not criticising the climate of this country. I myself took the liberty last year and the year before of pointing out why I thought the North-west Territories and the northern part of British Columbia were well adapted for settlement, and I have on other occasions pointed out why I think that northern Ontario, in future, when opened up from the colonization view point, will afford homes and employment for many thousands of people. Nor have we criticised the people of the country as some hon. gentlemen have endeavoured to do. We recognize that the people of the maritime provinces and of Quebec as well as of the whole of Canada are amongst the best that the world has produced with rare exceptions from the immigration view point in recent years, which I shall not refer to here. Therefore, I shall proceed to show the objections that we have to this scheme.
Nine months or a year ago an item appeared in a Minneapolis paper-and I think it was telegraphed to some of the Canadian papers-to the effect that the Senator referred to by the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals was about to exploit a new scheme. It was stated that he had attempted to become a member of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and that, having failed in that attempt, he was going to launch a scheme which involved the extension of the Grand Trunk Railway from its connections with St. Paul and Minneapolis into Winnipeg, from which point it would carry its main line to the Pacific coast, with branches all over Manitoba and the North-west Territories. Application was made to the legislature of Manitoba, and the newspapers in the city of Winnipeg, one with its whole front page, I remember, showed the plan of this great railway scheme ; and the name of the Hon. George Cox was mentioned publicly in the press and on the streets as being prominently connected with it. The reasons why that gentleman had

formed an alliance with the Grand Trunk and was pressing forward this scheme were almost semi-officially given. The plan was that the railway was to be entirely independent of either of the great western Canadian roads, the Canadian Northern or the Canadian Pacific. It was to extend from the Grand Trunk terminus in Chicago to Minneapolis, by controlling one of the American roads ; and, if the facts were known, I have no doubt that it would be found that the Grand Trunk Railway has to-day control of a line into the city of Minneapolis and into the city of St. Louis. It would not be polmc to let it be known, however, that the Grand Trunk is so near the Canadian border in the North-west until this Bill is passed. There was to be a branch built from the line between Minneapolis and Winnipeg to Duluth, to connect by a fleet of steamers witli the Midland system of the Grand Trunk, and become their principal grain line. It was announced at that time that the project was to have the endorsation of the Canadian parliament, almost identical with the endorsation this scheme is receiving here to-day. I want to say that I regard that as a very good scheme. I have no objection to it whatever. If the Grand Trunk Company would be content to accept a fair endorsation of a scheme which is only partly Canadian, I am not one to oppose it. I do not think, however, that such a scheme should get anything like the support that would be due to a scheme which would to a greater extent develop the Dominion of Canada. Some said that the object of all that demonstration was merely to force the Canadian Northern Railway Company to surrender.
No surrender !

No surrender was their motto, I believe, and I understand that no surrender is their motto to-day. Hon. members know that during this session items appeared in papers in the United States and also in the Montreal papers, to the effect that the Canadian Northern was about to surrender ; and this rumour was kept constantly before the public until only a few weeks ago. But, Sir, they came to the conclusion that the Canadian Northern Company could not be got to surrender, and they tacked on the patriotic end of the scheme, and the next move was that the Grand Trunk Company were going to extend their line from North Bay or Graven-hurst, paralleling the proposed line of the Canadian Northern to Winnipeg, and proceeding thence across the country to the coast. Still the coon did not come down. I presume that the hon. Minister of Justice happened to get wind of what was going on ; and, not content with the line from North Bay to Winnipeg, he saw a chance to secure some benefit for the friends of the Quebec bridge and some little encouragement for the province of Quebec ; and the
next proposition was that the line should run from the city of Quebec, through northern Quebec and Northern Ontario, to Winnipeg. Still another move was made, and our friends the enemy from the maritime provinces took a hand in, with the result that we now have the proposition for a road from Moncton to the city of Winnipeg, and thence onward to the coast. This is called the short line extension to Moncton. I regret that the right hon. First Minister is not in his place. I have always had the highest respect for that right hon. gentleman, both as a citizen and as a member of the House of Commons ; and when I heard that some transcontinental railway scheme was being evolved, I had perfect confidence in my own mind that the right hon. gentleman, in whose patriotism I have always had faith, though I never knew what his business capacity was, would produce a scheme that would at all events have a few clauses in it to commend it to this House and the country. I regret, Sir, that I have been disappointed. So far as the Grand Trunk Railway is concerned, I am not opposing that company. I regard Mr. Hays, its general manager, as one of the greatest railway men in the world ; I regard our old friend Mr. Wainwright as one of the most genial of men ; I regard Mr. Mc-Guigan as one of the ablest railway construction men in North America ; and the venerable Senator is a life-long friend of mine. So that if my personal feelings were to decide the matter, they would certainly lead me to support any scheme with which these gentlemen were connected. But I find in this scheme a pretense to build up our Canadian seaports, when I will show before I get through that its traffic will go to Portland, Boston and other American centres. They profess to reduce rates, when I venture to say that those who live ten or fifteen years hence will bear out my statement that not one cent per bushel'will be taken from the cost of the transportation of wheat through this proposal. They profess to solve the transportation problem, when they only confuse it. They profess to serve the interests of Canada, when they will load the people down with a burden which our children's children will not be free from, and which will tie the country up for many a long year to come. Many see in this scheme all sorts of jobs. It undoubtedly means the ruin of the Intercolonial as a national work. It means the burdening of this country with many hundreds of thousands of dollars annually for the maintenance of that road, because its earning power will be greatly diminished as soon as this new line is constructed. We see in this proposed line an attempt to make the Quebec bridge profitable : and, if I am informed aright, that bridge has already cost as much money as the plans and specifications indicated that the whole bridge would cost, although the

piers are scarcely above the water yet. I wonder what the upshot will be when the government blow a few more millions into it. It will undoubtedly be well watered. By this scheme they are side-tracking the city of Toronto in the province of Ontario, as well as the city of Montreal and all the southern part of the province of Quebec ; and yet, when the facts of the case are known, the city of Quebec will not receive from it so much benefit .as the gentlemen would have us believe. The question naturally arises, who has perpetrated this job ? Who. has delivered this gold brick to the Prime Minister ? There is undoubtedly a certain clamour about the transcontinental roa'd, but I do not think that alone would be sufficient to justify the celerity displayed by the right lion, the Prime Minister and a number of his colleagues, in whom many of us have had every confidence. The ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) said that the fact of the matter was that Senator Cox could not wait. Well, where was our friend the Minister of Labour and Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock)? Some suppose that he, rising above postage stamps and dabbling in labour problems, looks about for a vaster field in which to exercise his great genius, and has visions of being the leader of the great Liberal party in Canada in the near future. Some suppose that he is endeavouring to supplant the Minister of Finance and is really the father of this scheme. Others maintain that it is the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) who, with the energy of his race, wishes not only to be the leader in his native province, but the leader of the party in the Dominion. Certainly we have not yet any precise knowledge as to who the father of the scheme really is.
The scheme, at all events, is devoid of merit. It consists of two branches. The branch to the east from Winnipeg will not be constructed for at least ten years. It will not benefit Ontario or the city of Montreal or the maritime provinces, and I would, therefore, appeal to the Postmaster General to take the first minister in hand-if the hon. gentleman is not endorsing the scheme as its father-and induce the right hon. gentleman to withdraw it before the country is irrevocably committed to it. What are the details of the scheme ? There is to be nominally a government road from Moncton, in the province of New Brunswick, to Winnipeg, passing by the St. John valley, crossing at Quebec, onward through the northern part of Quebec and the northern part of Ontario, as far as Winnipeg. This section is to be built and owned by the government, but leased to the Grand Trunk Railway. It will pass 250 miles north of Montreal, over 400 miles north of Toronto, and from 120 to 180 miles north of Port Arthur and Fort William. That part of the road will be 1,900 miles long, and it will

cost anywhere from $60,000,000 to $80,000, 000 to construct. Then the next division, from Winnipeg to the Rockies to be assisted to the extent of $13,000 per mile, and through the Rockies to the coast to the extent of $30,000 a mile, and the government is to pay all the interest for a period of ten years, and give the company all the station lands, frontage, ports and harbours and terminals it requires. This section from Winnipeg to the coast will be absolutely the property of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway.
After fifty years the lease of the eastern part terminates, and supposing this to be the honest scheme, hon. gentlemen opposite would have us believe it is, at the end of fifty years the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will find themselves with a line stopping at Winnipeg. But the fact is that this is only a pretense, and the real scheme is as I shall show. The Grand Trunk Railway is now in the city of Chicago, and undoubtedly has arrangements made whereby it can readily get entrance into Minneapolis. It will then only be 470 miles from Winnipeg. It purposes building into Winnipeg, and will own a through-line from Portland, in Maine, to Port Simpson, on the Pacific coast. It will have a branch to Duluth, and that branch will connect with the Port of Midland, as a lake and rail route for grain. Now, the distance is not so very terrible after all, and it will be a magnificent road with a perfect road-bed, and I doubt whether it would be possible to get a finer transcontinental road. From Portland to Montreal the distance is 298 miles, thence to Chicago 840 miles, thence to Minneapolis, 420 miles, on to Winnipeg, 471 miles, and thence to Port Simpson, 1,600, making a total mileage from Portland to Winnipeg of 2,029, from Montreal to Winnipeg, of 1,731, and from Portland to Fort Simpson, of 3,600 odd miles. There is the transcontinental Grand Trunk Railway scheme. It is a scheme that I would heartily endorse, were it not that I object to the price we are paying for it. The North Shore line is absolutely not in the mind of the Grand Trunk Railway. The Grand Trunk Railway do not care a farthing about it. That company may put up its little guarantee, but it never intends running a line north of the lakes. Our lion, friend who preceded me pointed out, as one of the grand clauses of this contract, section 10, which provides as follows :
The work of locating and constructing the said western division shall be commenced forthwith after the ratification of this agreement by the parliament of Canada and shall proceed with the utmost despatch and be completed within five years from the first day of December. 1903.
What does that mean ? One year from that date, or one year from the passage of this Bill, the Grand Trunk Railway will have a certain number of miles of its own road built. What will it do with its freight?

Store it in Winnipeg ? At the end of two years, it will be a good way on to Ed-mundston. What will it do with its freight ? In three years it will be over the mountains. AVhat will it do with its freight V And in five years, when it will have reached the Pacific ocean, what will it then do with its freight ? As regards the road north of the lakes, from Moncton to Winnipeg, the surveys will not be completed at the end of the five years, much less the road constructed, and in the meantime where are you going to deliver all the freight that will have gathered along the line in the west ? The grain freight will simply go down by the Grand Trunk Railway to Duluth, and the passenger and ordinary traffic will go via Chicago to Portland. That is the plan of the Grand Trunk Railway. The only thing I object to is that these .men have not the honesty to tell the House that that is their plan. I am surprised the Grand Trunk Railway do not come up and let us know that that is their honest plan. The advantages of this route are many. In winter time, from one. end to the other, with the exception of a very few miles at this end and in the mountains of British Columbia, it will be free from snow. From one end of that road to the other, by the time Mr. McGuigan gets his grades completed throughout the province of Ontario-and he is about done with them now-the Grand Trunk Railway will have a small grade of about one-half per cent, and the finest road-bed in the world. From one end of the road to the other, there will be local traffic passing from Boston and the other cities on the sea coast and the cities and towns of Ontario and the interior of the United States-especially the great city of Chicago-and with its lines to St. Louis, the Grand Trunk Railway transcontinental system will be able to originate at local points more traffic for a through-line than any other transcontinental road on the continent ? It will also be a through-route, and there is no other route crossing the Rocky mountains in the United States which could begin to compare with it in distance and speed on account of the magnificent road-bed which it will have. More than that, from one end of that road to the other, coal and other necessary railway supplies would be found close by, and that, Sir, is a matter of great importance to a railway company crossing the continent. There is the scheme. No man who knows anything about the business believes, for one second, that anything else is the scheme; and the government need not attempt to befool us into believing that the Grand Trunk Railway Company would commit themselves to such a job as the general tenor of the resolutions would lead us to suppose. That is really estimating the intelligence of this House at too low a standard. If the Grand Trunk Railway, instead of building its line to Duluth, would build it to Port Arthur or Fort 'William, I would be willing it should
be liberally assisted. If the Grand Trunk Railway wanted assistance for a line from Wininpeg to Port Simpson, even a line that would not be looked upon as a national road, I do not believe that this country would object to giving it legitimate assistance.
Of course, I presume that the promoter of the road, the master mind, the genius, whoever he may be, who is behind this whole business, whether it is the senator or one of the ministers, or the man in control of the Grand Trunk, will be quite willing to accept a railway 1,900 miles long, built by the people of Canada, and maintained by them for fifty years, as a little gift. But that is not the main scheme. To show what their intention is, I have referred to section 10 to show that the western end must be built in five years and they must find an outlet for their traffic. I will now turn to section 42 to show that in it these gentleman show their hand to some extent. Section 42 says :
It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade and the transportation of goods through Canadian channels. The company accept the aid on these conditions, and agrees that all freight originating on the line of railway or its branches

Miud you this line originates in Canada and does not touch foreign soil from Port Simpson to the Atlantic seaboard.
-not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall, when destined to points in Canada be carried entirely on Canadian territory, or between Canadian inland ports, and that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports, and that all such traffic not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper shall be carried to Canadian ocean ports.
Will you tell me, Mr. Speaker, how they are going to carry it any other way if they do not intend to have a route through the States. How are they going to get it there any other way or how are they going to get it to any other port unless they intend to have a route through the United States? Undoubtedly, clause 10 and clause 42 together show clearly as the sun that they intend to have an American road. And it is equally clear that the government lawyers or the cabinet must have been very dense in making this contract, or else they are a party to it all. I have already pointed out the time it will take to construct this eastern road. I venture to say it will be ten years before it will be constructed, after which they have it free for seven years, and after that' for three years, the amount they are to be charged for interest will be added to the capital account. I presume. Mr. Speaker, that you and I will be taking a perpendicular look at the business by the

time they are ready to begin paying anything.
IJp or down ?

Down, always down. I shall not at the present time refer to the clause respecting running rights other than to say that any one who knows anything about railroading sees through it and smiles at it. But I will venture to say that, in case the northern line is constructed, and the Grand Trunk Pacific operates it- I am at liberty to put in these provisos, because one of the chief clauses of the contract I find punctured with provisos-the charges for freight in Grand Trunk cars and Grand Trunk Pacific cars running over the government section will more than pay the rental that would be charged against the company. Section 37 was pointed out by my predecessor, who said this was a specially strong clause in the contract. I would like my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) as a Canadian manufacturer to consider, and I want all Canadian producers to consider, how they are going to be benefited by this clause.
The company shall purchase all material and supplies required for the construction of the western division and the equipment of the whole of the said line of railway from Canadian producers-
And when the hon. gentleman had read that far, he looked around as though to say, ' This is the place for you to cheer me.' And then he read the rest :
-when the same are produced in Canada and where such material and supplies can he purchased in desired quantities and of equal quality suitable for the purpose required, and for prices and upon terms equally advantageous with those procurable elsewhere.
How much are our Canadian producers going to sell on that western section if it does not suit these gentlemen to buy ? But that point has been handled before. I shall not take it up. Now as to the clause guaranteeing the running rights. Is it to be supposed for a second that the Grand Trunk owning a line absolutely from Portland to Winnipeg, and owning a line of the Grand Trunk Pacific from Winnipeg to Port Simpson, are going to ruin their property or cause its deterioration by running a pound of freight over the road owned by the government and in which they have no interest, sending the freight to Moncton, and thence under a separate agreement to the sea ? The general surface of this area may also he characterized as rolling, though sometimes rising into ridges and mountains. Traversing this area in the north-east and south-west direction are wide belts of granite and pre-Cambrian rocks which usually have a greater elevation than the formations on either side. The country through which they extend is mostly in a forest-clad, widerness condition and unfit for settlement. No well defined range of mountains exists in this part of the province, but denuded remnants of that spur or lateral extension of the Appalachian system across it in the north-western part and are to be seen in Mars hill, just west of the International boundary, 1,688 feet above sea level according to the boundary survey, and Moose mountain, east of the St. John, 1,490 feet in height, with other hills about the sources of Munquart river and to the east. Now, we will transfer our attention to the west. We are told that the west is up in arms for this transcontinental road. What is the agitation about ? We had good crops for the last two or three years in the Northwest, a great many new farmers went into the country, and very few of them had granaries. The railways and the grain buyers had very few elevators at the stations, and as a consequence there was a glut in getting the grain out, and there was a great outcry in the country. I think it is a good advertisement for the country in that way, and perhaps those who are interested in the development of the west may not be sorry for it. However, the chief causes of difficulty were that we had abundant crops and the farmers who had more recently settled had not granaries built for its accommodation, so that they had to market the grain in the fall and the railway facilities were not sufficient to get it out in a rush. These grievances have to a large extent been removed. Many of the farmers have in the last two or three years improved their facilities for warehousing grain, and the elevator men have built elevators all over the country sufficient to accommodate many million more bushels of wheat than was formerly the case. It is also a fact that the railways have greatly improved their transport facilities, as well as their facilities for handling grain at Lake Superior ports. In consequence there will not be any great difficulty in handling grain in the future. There is another condition of things which bears to an important extent on the question of the marketing of our grain. I find from the United States report of the Bureau of Industries that in the year 1900 they produced
522,000,000 bushels of wheat, and yet on the first of March, 1901, the farmers held in their granaries out of that crop 128,000,000 bushels, which shows that the farmers in the United States do not rush out their grain in the fall, or in the winter, or even in the early spring, but that they keep it and watch for a rise in the market to sell it to advantage. At the date I have mentioned there were 87,000,000 bushels of grain only in the elevators east of the Rocky mountains, and in this calculation I do not include the 36,000,000 that are raised west of the Rocky mountains. I take the Duluth rate, and if our country develops as we expect it will develop, that rate should prevail in Canada; I find that the rate from Winnipeg to Port Arthur is 10 cents a hundred pounds, or 6 cents a bushel ; from Port Arthur to Buffalo 2 cents ; from Buffalo to New York, via the Erie canal, 4 cents, which makes a total of 12 cents from Winnipeg to the city of New York. The ocean rate varies from 2 to 7 cents, depending on the season of the year ; but, at all events, if you take the ocean rate of 4 or 41 cents, you have your grain transported from Winnipeg to Liverpool for 16 cents a bushel, and the people of the town of Lindsay pay very nearly that for the grain which they ship to the city of Montreal. The point I want to make is that freight rates are not controlled by railways, but that the water routes are the controlling influences in connection with freight rates. The rate from Chicago to Buffalo, all rail, in 1902, was 11J cents per 100 pounds, or 7* cents per bushel. Compare that with the all-water route from Chicago to Buffalo,. one and three-fifths to two and three-eights, or an average of one and a half cents a bushel, and you find that the grain by the water haul is five and seven-tenths cents per bushel from Chicago to Buffalo. Take the all-rail route from Chicago to New York during 1902, which was from seventeen and a half to twenty cents per hundred pounds. The exact figure for that year, as given by the Chicago Board of Trade, was 10-62 cents per bushel. That is the exact cost by the all-rail route from Chicago to New York. Take the water route, and I want to point out that the low figure is brought about by competition with the Lake Erie canal. His situation and the line of his duty may he seen by considering how soldiers ought to act in the following cases.
An officer orders his oldiers in a time of political excitement then and there to arrest and shoot without trial a popular leader against whom no crime has been proved, but who is suspected of treasonable designs. He read two passages of it, and only two, clauses 37 and 42. Let me refer, first, to clause 37. Well, will he be surprised to learn-I do not know whether he ought to be surprised, because I am sure it has already been pointed out in this House-that the very section in this Bill which has excited the hon. gentleman's criticisms and his friends' hilarity, is exactly the section which was moved by the hon. member for Cornwall as an amendment to the Bill incorporating the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. I shall read tlie two sections side by side, and I give my hon. friend the benefit of the comparison ; and if he can show anything in this Bill, which is more of a limitation than what is contained in the resolution of the hon. member for Cornwall (Mr. Pringle), then I will do what be himself offered to do a moment ago, and resign my seat and let him come and have it, if lie wants it.
And can get it.

Of course, always subject to that limitation. Clause 37 of the contract reads :
The company shall purchase all material and supplies for the construction of the western division and the equipment of the whole of the said line of railway from Canadian producers, when the same are produced in Canada

I want to know if the hon. gentleman thinks the company should be obliged to purchase them in Canada if they are not produced in Canada.
-and when such materials and supplies can be purchased in desired quantities and of equal quality suitable for the purposes required -
I do not suppose that the hon. gentleman would want to have the railway company bound to purchase materials and supplies from Canadian producers when they are not produced in Canada, and when they are not suitable for the purposes required. No one is going to consent that goods, whether Canadian or American or from any other part of the world, may be put into the railway unless suitable for the purposes required;
-and for prices and upon terms equally advantageous to those procurable elsewhere.

Would it be reasonable to ask this company, which is putting its money into the building of 3,000 or 4,000 miles of railway, that they should purchase their supplies in Canada when such supplies were not suitable for the purposes required and could not be got for prices and upon terms equally advantageous with those procurable elsewhere ? Surely those are entirely reasonable and proper qualifications on which to impose on the company the obligation of purchasing goods in the Canadian market. But if there be anything wrong in this clause it is taken directly and absolutely from the resolution moved by the hon. member for Cornwall (Mr. Pringle.)
Read the resolution of the hon. member for Cornwall.

I am about to read it. It is as follows :
In the event of any subsidies being granted to the said company,' they shall be subject to the conditions that the company shall, as far as practicable

Now, if the shoe were on the other foot, how we could ring the changes on that. You can take any meaning you like out of it. What is the meaning of ' as far as practicable ' ?
-construct, equip and operate their line or lines of railway with railway supplies, structural iron and steel, railway fastenings and cement and rolling stock of Canadian manufacture, whenever such railway supplies and rolling stock can be procured as cheaply and upon as good terms in Canada as elsewhere, having regard to quality and price among other things.
Which is the most hazy and indefinite? This one leaves the decision to the arbitrary discretion of the company, and I do not hesitate to say that clause 37 leaves less open to the company than this clause 40, which was to be added to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Bill.
In one of them the articles are defined and not in the other.

That is true ; I was forgetting to mention it. This proposition of the hon. member for Cornwall only relates to particular articles, but the clause we have put in the contract applies to any articles of any kind. That distinction was in my mind, but I forgot to mention it, and I am very grateful to my hon. friend for having reminded me of it. It certainly shows that the clause we have inserted is more comprehensive than the other.
There is another section of this Bill to Which the hon. gentleman refers, and that is the one which, of all others, he says shows the cloven hoof. That is section 42 :
It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties to this agreement, that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade and the transportation of goods through Canadian

channels. The company accepts the aid on these conditions, and agrees that all freight originating on the line of the railway or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shippers, shall, when destined for points in Canada, be carried entirely on Canadian territory or between Canadian inland ports.
Ha, ha, the hon. members say. Just look at that, does not that show the cloven hoof ? If they were not intending to have the control of roads on the American territory, why would they have put that there ? It is a circumstance of the greatest possible suspicion that they have it there. But then it would have been cited as a circumstanc of the greatest possible suspicion if they did not have it there ; so, it does not make much difference, so far as that is concerned, whether they have it there or not. If we had said nothing about sending it over Canadian territory, the hon. gentleman would hav said :	Why do you not have a clause pro
viding that this traffic is to be carried al together over Canadian territory ? The Minister of Justice properly and naturally put it there, and now it is regarded as terribly suspicious that it is there. I have never heard or read of an argument of thi character since Sergeant Buzfuzz showed the unutterable things that were concealed in the message about chops and tomato sauce. Now, Just one word more on this point. I want to know why the hon. gen tleman did not finish the reading of that clause. It would have been fair and Just that he should have read the two lines at the end of the section :
-that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports, and that all such traffic, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper shall be carried by Canadian ocean ports.
I think that if the hon. gentleman had been desirous of making a fair and Just statement of the contract, if he had not been desirous of quibbling and endeavouring to pervert the meaning, if he had not desired to find some faults that did not exist, he would not have failed to go on, as he easily might, to show how clear and manifest the intention of the government was to compel them to make this road what it is destined to be, an all-Canadian route for the purpose of building up Canadian ports. And he would have read another section immediately after, which is to the effect that:
The company shall arrange for and provide, either by purchase, charter or otherwise, shipping connections upon both the Atlantic and Pacific oceans sufficient in tonnage and in number of sailings to take care of and transport all its traffic both inward and outward, at such ocean ports within Canada upon tie said line of railway, or upon the line of the Intercolonial Railway, as may be agreed upon from time to time, and the company shall not livert, or, so far as it can lawfully prevent permit to be diverted, to ports outside of Canada any traffic

which it can lawfully Influence or control, upon the ground that there is not a sufficient amount of shipping to transport such traffic from or to such Canadian ocean ports.
Now, I say that these two clauses taken together make it absolutely clear that this is to be a Canadian line to be worked in the interest of Canadian ports. And I say that all that is necessary to make it a truly Canadian line, and all that it is necessary for us to assume as existing to ensure its complete success are, in our eastern ports, some little degree of push, and in our western country some little degree of patriotism. With patriotism at the western end and push at the eastern end, it is absolutely certain that this will be a transcontinental line that must build up the ports of our country. Because the patriotic man in the west will route his traffic through Canadian ports, and the Canadian ports will provide the means and facilities to handle it, and in this way the line cannot fail to be a truly Canadian transcontinental railway, serving well the purpose which it is the intention of the government and of this House that it should serve.
But my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) says that they are not going to work this line at all. Apparently the hon. gentleman lias not thought of the fact that they cannot help working it. He seems to think that this is something that they can take or leave at their own will. He evidently does not know any more about the terms of this contract than do some of his legal friends who criticise it. The company is bound under contract to take the lease of this road for fifty years-there is no option on their part. They are bound not only to take the road, but to work it. But he says that Mr. Hays is a far-seeing man, there is no limit to the amount of iiis brain and the length of his head ; and Mr. Hays has deliberately entered into an agreement looking ahead for fifty years, and at the end of that time, is going to throw up his road and then carry the grain to Minneapolis, or Chicago, or Philadelphia, or Portland, or wherever else it is the hon. gentleman sug gests-somewhere that is not a Canadian port. Well, I knew that Mr. Hays was a pretty long-headed man. He certainly has that reputation. But if he is so long-headed that he is entering into this contract thinking of what he will do fifty years hence when most of us will be in our graves, he is longer-headed than even the greatest of admirers gave him credit for being. The hon. gentleman was even a little more im aginative, and told us he was not going to work this road. But the contract says they must take it and they must work it. Of course, one point I will concede to the hon gentleman-we do not expect the company to work this road until the road is ready We all must admit that. Nobody supposes that they can be called upon to run their trains over the road until the sleepers are down and the rails laid. But when the road
is ready, the contract obliges the company to work it. And the hon. gentleman himself has shown in the most conclusive way that they can work it, because he has demonstrated that a matter of three or four hund red miles more or less In the length of a , great railway does not make any difference in rates. That is the fact. Anybody who knows anything about railroads has had that fact brought to his attention. For in stance, Portland is a northern port. It is further from the great centres of distribution than Boston. Farther still from those centres than New York, and farther still than Baltimore. Yet, an added distance of two or three hundred miles-the hon gentleman said three or four hundred miles- does not make any difference in the rates on the long haul. If that be the case-and it is the case when you come to continental distances, such as three or four thousand miles. That is exactly why this great transcontinental railway company would be able to carry this grain over the road we are going to build for them. Even if Halifax or St. John may be much farther away from Winnipeg or Port Simpson than Portland will be, yet it will be practically the same thing for them to carry to Halifax ' r St. John over the long distance as to carry to Portland. And we rely for the proof of that proposition upon the very demonstration which the hon. gentleman has made that this increased distance is a negligible quantity.
Then why don't you use the Intercolonial ?

The Intercolonial is a different thing altogether. It is a short piece of railway which does not connect with the grain centres of the west, and the principle does not apply to a short line as it does to a long line.
The hon. gentleman referred to the matter of running powers, but dealt with it with extreme lightness-as lightly as light could be. He said that so far as running powers were concerned, every body has read that provision, and every body smiles at it. But every body does not smile at it. Some people think it a matter of very great importance. Mr. Hudson wrote a book on railways to demonstrate the great inequality and difficulties and injustices connected with the administration of railway systems in the United States, and he said that the right method for removing these difficulties and extortions was to restore the original theory of a railway highway, as is being done, to a large extent, in this very Bill. My hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) the other day demonstrated from actual fact that the railway highway theory is not an impracticable idea ; he demonstrated that it is not only a workable theory, but a working theory. This writer shows why he had a working theory, and these are his words :

Manifestly, to let any one run engines or cars over any railway, free from supervision or direction, would produce hopeless wreck and disorder.
The Duke of Wellington said we must never forget the analogy of a highway. Railways in England were built upon the analogy of highways, and this argument is that if we are going to have a proper definition of a railroad, we must work back to the old theory of the highway.
Such a proposition would be presumptive of lunacy. But when we inquire whether a plan cannot be perfected which shall retain all needful precautions, and enforce by law the authority of the central officer over trains in motion, while giving to carriers the right to compete in the carriage of freight, the question assumes a very different aspect. What is there in these methods which cannot be preserved without the exclusive privilege of carrying freight over the track ? The maintenance of schedules need not interfere with the freedom of competition. The carrier wishing to run a train of his own could he required to run a regular train on schedule time, or to follow a regular train with an extra, just as extras are now run on every railroad in the country. The control of the trains in motion must be given to a train-despatcher ; but the trains thus controlled may be owned, loaded, and forwarded by different carriers.
He did not see anything impossible about it.
If the law secures implicit obedience to the orders of the train-despatcher, while the trains are on the railway, can it make any difference to the safety and speed of the service that one train is owned by A, another by B, and that both carry freight at such rates as are fixed by free competition ? Cannot the authority which controls the trains be made as absolute and unquestioned as now, or even more so, without vesting the monopoly of transportation in a single company ? Cannot the obedience of the men in charge of the trains, and their intelligence and care, be. secured in as high a degree if competing carriers are allowed to use the same track ? And cannot the use of safe rolling-stock and its maintenance in good repair, by frequent inspections, be enforced just as well under a system of competition as under a system of monopoly ? These are the questions which must be answered, in order to determine whether the idea of competition in transportation over the same track is practicable.
This proposition does not contemplate sending a number of trains under conflicting control upon the same track. It simply proposes that the right of outside carriers to load their trains, at whatever rates they choose, and to send them over the tracks of the railway, shall be established, under whatever regulations are necessary for the preservation of speed and safety ; and asserts that all these regulations can be enforced consistently with the practice of free competition. The first condition that it assumes is, that all such competing trains would he started on schedule time, and fun either as regular trains, or as extra trains following the regular ones. It next supposes, as a vital condition, that all trains will be under the control of the train-despatcher from the moment that they come upon the track until they reach their destination. All the details cf reporting the progress of each train, at every Mr. RUSSELL.
telegraph station which it passes, of keeping the record of its location in the central office, and of governing its movements by telegraphic orders, can be enforced as well, whether the trains are owned by a single corporation or by a dozen. Let the law, or the rules of the railway company, provide absolute control by the train-despatcher, of trains in motion, and the efficiency of that officer need not be in any respect diminished by the fact that the trains are owned and laden by competing carriers.
Mr. Hudson goes the whole length of saying that any number of companies can run their cars over the same road, but his theory is that that road ought to be owned by the state. I do not press the theory that far, the government does not press it that far. All they are saying is that one or two companies can have the use of this road besides the Grand Trunk Company; that all the great companies that want to carry grain out of the North-west or anything else may feasibly and advantageously be allowed to use it on fair and equal terms, and that is what the government propose to do between Winnipeg and Moncton.
Have any great railway experts adopted those views ?
Here is one who has adopted that view.
He is not a railway expert, he is a railway theorist.

What are experts but theorists ? I will give my hon. friend another opinion, that, of a gentleman who ha's considered the railroad question seriously and technically, and that is ex-Governor Larrabee of Iowa, who says :
The adoption of Mr. Hudson's plan would simply be a return to the first principle of railroad transportation. It has already been shown that the first English charters permitted the public to use their own vehicles and motive power upon the railroad track, but that shippers and independent carriers could not avail themselves of these provisions of the early charters because it was in the power of the railroad companies to make their tolls prohibitory. There is but little question as to the practicability of Mr. Hudson's plan from a purely technical standpoint, and its adoption might be advisable if it should be demonstrated that a monopoly of the track is inconsistent with the operation of the railways for the public good.
That is to say, ex-Governor Larrabee sees no technical difficulty in the matter at all, he considers it feasible but doubts if it would have the beneficial effect which Mr. Hudson anticipated from its operation. Now, I give the opinions of these two authorities. I do not think that railway experts would go the length of saying that it would be desirable or safe that everybody should be allowed to pass a train upon the track and at a fixed toll. I do not think that would feasible. But in the estimation of two such eminent authorities as Mr. Hudson and ex-Governor Larrabee, what the hon. member for North Norfolk said is

amply justified when lie showed from actual experience that it is feasible for more than one railway authority to send its cars over the same line of road, as we know it is.
The hon. gentleman has quoted the member for North Norfolk as making a statement about the Wabash Railway, a statement which I deny.
It does not make any difference if the hon. gentleman does deny it, I am reasserting it. I have just as much faith in the hon. member for North Norfolk as I have in the hon. gentleman.
I may further state
Order.
I am asking the hon. gentleman's permission to make a statement.

I do not think it is worth while for us both to try to speak at the same time. There is one other matter that I wish to refer to, and that is the information the hon. gentleman gave us about the central route in the province of New Brunswick. Now, he has absolutely misunderstood, I think, the speech which was made by my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson). My hon. friend from Westmoreland made it clear that the route which was being referred to in Sir Sandford Fleming's report was a route that went up to Rivifire du Loup and over a chain of mountains, while the route that is proposed or contemplated by this Bill, is to be taken through the province of New Brunswick, and all the references that have been made to Sir Sandford Fleming's report and to the cross sections he mentions, are entirely beside the mark. It was made clear by my hon. friend from Westmoreland that the route which is contemplated runs from Quebec back of tbe mountains, which skirt the south shore of the St. Lawrence river, and passes around the border of the state of Maine and clown through the central part of New Brunswick, which is an entirely different line from that which is criticised in Sir Sandford Fleming's report. I have some more observations to make about that subject, but in the meantime, lest hon. members should go away with a false impression, I want to point out the fact that there was always a contention between Mr. Wilkinson, the provincial engineer of the province of New Brunswick, and Major Robinson, on whose report, to a large extent, Sir Sandford Fleming relied when he gave his account of this central route which ran partly through the province of New Brunswick and partly through Quebec, where we do not propose to go in this Bill at all. This road takes an entirely different course. So that the evidence my hon. friend quoted he has quoted to no purpose at all, and he might just as well have quoted from a book of logarithms. Mr. Wilkinson, in criticising the circuitous route that the Intercolonial Railway takes around the northern part of New Brunswick, in his contest with Major Robinson says :
Were a proposition now for the first time offered, that the intercourse between Halifax and Quebec should not pass through New Brunswick, except by the most circuitous route that could be made, it might justly be expected to be repugnant to both Nova Scotia and Canada. But it has, I trust, been shown, that such a proposition would be at least equally objectionable to New Brunswick, and that it is for the common interest that the inter-communication should be as direct as the natural facilities of the country will permit.
There is Mr. Wilkinson's evident impression. Mr. Wilkinson's impression and opinion which is evidently the opinion of the people in New Brunswick shows that the route which Major Robinson had recommended and along which the Intercolonial Railway now goes was a circuitous route, was too long a route, was longer than need be and that a route through the central part of New Brunswick was one which would give us as direct a route as the natural facilities of the country would permit. Now, Mr. Speaker, with this ref erence to the ques-ton of the location of the Intercolonial Railway and the saving to be effected by running it through the centre of the province of New Brunswick I have no further remark to make in regard to the speech of the hon. member for North Victoria and with the permission of the House I beg to move that the debate be now adjourned.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
